title: The enemies within and without
hook: the prayer asks for enemies to be ended; many read them also as the five thieves inside

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart's wish, and your line was the heart's wish itself. Did you find the deeper wish under a small one? Today the prayer turns to something harder. Day three hundred seventy-three.

Anandpur, in the last years of the sixteen hundreds. The town where the Tenth Guru lives sits in the hills, and the hills are full of trouble. Neighboring kings resent him. Imperial armies will later come. There will be sieges, hunger, a night when the town has to be left behind. These aren't metaphors. They're men with weapons, and they're coming. And in this world, the Guru writes a prayer that asks, plainly, for enemies to be ended. It's one of the lines people stumble over when they first read Chaupai. Today: the enemies within and without.
screen: `ANANDPUR, IN THE HILLS.` → `REAL ARMIES, REAL SIEGES.` → `A PRAYER ABOUT ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: The lines come right after the heart's wish. In paraphrase: destroy all my enemies; save me with your own hand. May my family live in peace, and all my servants and Sikhs. A little later: protect me with your own hand, and end all my foes this very day. The word for enemy here is dusht, the wicked, the one who means harm. Sikhs read these lines in two ways, and they don't have to choose. The first reading is the plain one. The Guru and his community faced real violence, and this is the prayer of a leader asking God to protect his people from those who would kill them. Sikhs don't apologize for that. Asking for protection from harm isn't hatred. The second reading goes inside. The Guru Granth Sahib speaks again and again of five thieves living in every person: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego. They break in at night, the scripture says, and rob the house of its treasure. Many Sikhs, saying Chaupai every day, hear the enemies as those five too. The dusht that does you the most harm on an ordinary Tuesday probably isn't an army. It's your own anger at the driver who cut you off, or the greed that keeps you scrolling, or the ego that can't say sorry. What's notable is where the prayer puts the fight. It doesn't say, let me destroy them. It says, you destroy them, and save me with your hand. The battle, inner or outer, is handed over. The enemy within doesn't go because you hate it. It goes when you're held by something stronger.
screen: `DESTROY MY ENEMIES; SAVE ME.` · `READING ONE: REAL ARMIES.` · `READING TWO: THE FIVE THIEVES.` · `YOU DESTROY THEM; HOLD ME.` · then, large: `END THE ENEMY WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one inner enemy. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego. Don't make a list of all your faults. Just notice which one has been busiest in you lately. Which one robbed you this week? Name it, simply, in one word. Then, instead of fighting it, picture handing it over, the way the prayer does. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do. If you don't, just let your grip on it loosen a little. The bell holds the time.
The enemies within and without. Chaupai's lines asking for enemies to be ended: real armies for the Guru, and for many Sikhs, the five thieves inside too.
screen: `THE ENEMIES WITHIN AND WITHOUT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: end the enemy within. Today, when the enemy you named shows up, notice it, name it under your breath, and hand it over before it takes anything. Day three hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these lines of Chaupai Sahib daily, understanding the enemies both as outward threats and as the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego.

fork.reveal: Chaupai hands the fight over: destroy all my enemies, save me with your hand. many Sikhs hear the same request against the five thieves within.

original.note: Gurmukhi: dusht, the wicked or the one who means harm; in Chaupai, the enemies the prayer asks God to end.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer asking for harm to come to enemies.
what it means: a plea for protection from real danger, and for many Sikhs, from the five thieves inside too.
what a scholar hears: by its traditional dating the poem comes from the years of tension around Anandpur, and Sikh commentary has long read its enemies on both levels, outward and inward.

sources.ref: five thieves (panj chor), a recurring image in the Guru Granth Sahib

notes: Verses paraphrased: 'hamre dusht sabhai tum ghaavahu, aap haath dai mohi bachaavahu; sukhee basai moro parivaaraa, sevak sikh sabhai kartaaraa' and 'mo rachhaa nij kar dai kariyai, sabh bairin ko aaj sanghariyai'. Confirm.

Historical setting: tensions with the hill rajas and later Mughal sieges of Anandpur, ending with the evacuation in 1704/1705. The voice keeps dates general ('the last years of the sixteen hundreds'). The trapdoor gives the traditional dating: Charitropakhyan's colophon is commonly given as 1753 Bikrami (1696 CE). Confirm.
Five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankar) and the image of thieves robbing the house: the Ang reference is a suggestion; Keeper to supply the best one.
Two readings presented as both held; confirm.
